tagline.text: A small museum of ancient wooden boats and old burials dug up in Butuan

location.label: Location
location.text: Libertad, Butuan City, Agusan del Norte (about 5 km west of the city center, on the road toward the airport)

children.text: The Balangay Shrine Museum is a small, partly open-air field museum that displays the ancient wooden balangay boats found in Butuan in 1976, along with wooden coffins and deformed skulls. A visit takes only an hour or two, so it fits easily into a day in Butuan.

The Balangay Shrine Museum is a small museum in Libertad, Butuan City, in northeastern Mindanao. Butuan sits at the mouth of the Agusan River, and the museum lies between the city and the airport, about
5 km

from the city center. It is known as a field museum run by the National Museum of the Philippines, and behind the building an actual excavation pit remains. The address is given as 6th St., Sitio Ambangan, but map apps list it under the name "Balangay Shrine Museum," so searching by name is the safer option.

What makes this museum special is the boat called the balangay (also spelled balanghai). The word refers to a seagoing wooden boat made of planks joined together and fastened with wooden pegs, and it is often cited as evidence that people in the Philippines have crossed the seas since ancient times. According to accounts, on September 6, 1976, looters searching for Chinese ceramics in the village of Ambangan, Butuan, found nine boats under the ground. So far three have been excavated, and the rest remain buried in place. The biggest draw is Butuan Boat No. 1, one of these boats, displayed inside a glass protective case.

The age of the boats is described a little differently depending on the source. Travel blogs and guides say the oldest boat was dated to 320 AD (reportedly by radiocarbon testing at Gakushuin University in Tokyo), while others came out at 990 AD and 1250 AD. Some of the same writing also gives 777–988 AD, so the numbers conflict, and it is safest to think of the boats as dating from somewhere between the 4th and the 13th centuries. For the most accurate answer, ask the staff at the museum which date is currently considered official.
The boat's length also varies by source. The balangays found in Butuan are described as averaging about
long and about
3 m
wide, while one visitor account gives the original length of Boat No. 1 as about

. Use the figures on the exhibit panels as your reference. This is not a large museum, so rather than making a long trip with big expectations, think of it as a place to spend an hour or two on a piece of history during a day in downtown Butuan.

This is the museum's centerpiece. The structure of planks joined edge to edge and fastened with wooden pegs is preserved in a glass case, so you can look closely at the seams. Woods such as toog, narig and lawaan are reported to have been identified in the boat, and sugar palm fiber is said to have been used to bind the planks. If a staff member is on hand, they will walk you through the structure.

Behind the building, one excavation pit where a boat was actually unearthed remains, giving you a sense of how it lay buried in the ground. The area is part of the Agusan River delta landscape. Another excavation site elsewhere in the city is reportedly not open to the public, so this pit is effectively the only one you can see in person.
A wooden coffin about
3 m

long and skulls are on display. The coffins are described as dating to the 14th–15th centuries and as having been found during the 1976 excavation. Some of the skulls show signs of the head having been deliberately pressed in childhood to flatten the forehead, which has been interpreted as a sign of group affiliation, social status or a taste for a certain look. Some accounts also say the coffins are not from the same period as the boat layer but belong to a separate layer found in higher ground.

The walls display photos of the 1976–1986 excavations along with the rope that once bound the planks. You can follow in chronological order how the boats found by looters led to a scholarly excavation. A few other finds, such as pottery fragments and jars, are also on display.

The balangay boats were declared a National Cultural Treasure under Presidential Proclamation No. 86. The land on which the museum stands is said to have been donated in 1979 by Felix A. Luna. Sources give different years for the declaration, so this guide does not state one.

In 2009, a replica balangay called "Diwata ng Lahi" is said to have been used in a voyage around the Philippines and Southeast Asia. It was built by boatbuilders from Sibutu and Sitangkai in Tawi-Tawi using traditional methods. We could not confirm whether the replica can be seen at the museum, so ask before you visit.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The museum and heritage sites in downtown Butuan

children.text: Take a tricycle or Grab from your hotel to the Balangay Shrine Museum in Libertad. It is quiet if you arrive around opening time.
Listen to the staff and see Butuan Boat No. 1, the wooden coffins and the skulls.
See the excavation pit behind the building and take photos.
Head back into town and visit the Butuan regional museum (the National Museum in Butuan) or St. Joseph Cathedral.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town and rest.
Getting around is mostly by tricycle or multicab, and the trip from downtown to the museum is about
15–25 minutes
. Opening hours differ from source to source, so it is a good idea to call the day before.

items.title: Full-day course in Butuan
items.subtitle: Ancient boats and the legend of Magellan's landing

children.text: Visit the museum first to learn about the balangay and the story of the excavation.
Walk around the downtown museum and the St. Joseph Cathedral area.
After lunch, look around Bood Promontory Eco Park or the site known as Magellan's landing site.
Finish the day along the Agusan River or at the Banza Church ruins, where only the bell tower and banyan trees remain.

Bood Promontory and the Magellan landing site are where the city commemorates Mazaua Discovery Day on March 31, but where the first Mass was held is disputed, since another account places it on Limasawa Island.
Airlines such as Cebu Pacific fly nonstop from Manila to Butuan Bancasi Airport (BXU), and the flight takes about
1 hour
. Airlines and schedules change with the season, so check when you book.
The airport is about
2 km
from downtown, and the museum is on the road between the airport and the city, so it is also a convenient stop right after you land. Taxis are available outside the airport security gate.
Routes and flight frequencies change often, so check the latest schedule before you leave.
From Cagayan de Oro the trip by bus such as Bachelor Express is reported to take about
8 hours
, and from Davao about
6 hours
(fares were reported at about ₱400–490, but confirm locally). Long-distance buses from Manila also run.
Ferries arrive at the port of Nasipit, about
27 km
west of downtown. Operators such as 2GO, Cokaliong, Lite Ferries and Trans-Asia are listed, but schedules need to be checked.
The museum is about
5 km
from downtown (for example, around Gaisano Mall or the integrated terminal). You can take a tricycle directly, or ride a jeepney or multicab marked "Libertad" and then transfer to a tricycle.
A 2016 visitor account lists the tricycle fare as about ₱8, but today's fare may differ greatly, so confirm before you ride. If you can get a Grab, it is even easier.
In Butuan, multicabs and tricycles are the main means of transport, and taxis can be found at the large shopping malls and in front of the airport.
If you plan to visit several places in one day, it is easier to negotiate a tricycle or taxi by the half day.
The museum is small and partly open-air, so on rainy days the excavation pit can be uncomfortable to view. The Agusan River basin gets frequent rain, so the dry season is the safer choice.

Around March 31, the city holds events for Mazaua Discovery Day, and during city events such as Adlaw hong Butuan on August 2 and the city fiesta on May 9, downtown can get crowded. Event dates change each year, so check the city government's announcements.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Relatively cool, though some months are rainy
Fine for sightseeing and walking downtown, but bring an umbrella
Mornings are best for the outdoor excavation pit
Open-air viewing can be uncomfortable, so combine it with indoor stops

items.label: Museum admission
items.note: A 2013 visitor account says free (donations welcome); the National Museum announced free admission and Monday-to-Sunday opening for its museums from 2025, but whether this field museum follows it needs confirming

items.label: Tricycle (downtown to museum)
items.note: About ₱8 per a 2016 account, but subject to change

items.label: Airport to downtown
items.note: About 2 km, by taxi or multicab

items.label: Accommodation
items.note: Guesthouses from the ₱200s to hotels in the ₱2,000s are listed

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

Accommodation is concentrated in downtown Butuan. Wikivoyage lists mid-range and large hotels such as Almont Inland Resort, Balanghai Hotel, Almont City Hotel, Go Hotels Butuan and Watergate Hotel, along with budget places at roughly ₱120–700. Hotel rates change greatly with the season, so check the latest reviews and prices on a booking site. Almont Inland Resort is described as about
15 minutes
from the museum by car.

Dining centers on the restaurants of downtown Butuan. The place Wikivoyage picks out is "RIBBS," known for barbecued ribs and seafood, and mall food courts are also convenient. Assume there are no large restaurants around the museum, and it is better to eat in town before heading out. A distillery that makes laksoy, a wine made from nipa palm, is listed as a local specialty, but check the taste and hygiene for yourself.
The museum is small, so an hour or two is enough. Combine it with other heritage sites in downtown Butuan for a half-day or full-day plan.
Opening hours differ by source. A 2024 visitor account says Tuesday to Sunday,
(closed Mondays), the National Museum announced Monday-to-Sunday opening for its regional museums from 2025 (not confirmed for this field museum), while another source gives
, so call before you go.
A mobile number, (0919) 077-9854, and the email butuan@nationalmuseum.gov.ph have been listed as contacts, but whether they are still current needs confirming.
Staff members often explain the exhibits on site, so treat numbers such as dates and sizes according to the panels and what the staff tell you.
The excavation pit is outdoors, so bring a folding umbrella or a light rain jacket in case of a shower.
If admission is free or low, there may be a donation box for conservation, so keep some small change.
The regional museum nearby (the National Museum in Butuan) has its own opening days and fees, so do not confuse the two.
Opening hours and admission differ between sources, so you may make the trip for nothing. It may be closed on Mondays, so be sure to check before you set out.
Numbers such as boat length and age differ between sources, so the figures on the panels at the site take priority.
The area around the bus terminal is crowded and there is a risk of pickpockets, so keep your belongings in front of you.
The exhibits include glass cases and protected areas, so do not touch them or lean on them, and ask the staff about photography rules.
The cost and hours information in this guide covers what was confirmed in several visitor accounts and may change over time. Check the latest announcements.
The city is about
5 km
from the museum. In
Butuan Heritage City
you can see St. Joseph Cathedral and the regional museum on foot.
This regional museum run by the National Museum is described as showing stone tools, metalwork, woodwork, ceramics, goldsmith work and wooden coffins in its archaeological hall.
Known as the place where the city of Butuan claims Magellan's party raised a cross and held the first Mass, it is described as having a tree park and a view of the Masao River.
The site of a church said to have been built by the Recollect order in 1625 and destroyed by Moro pirates in 1753, where the bell tower and banyan trees remain.
Described as the longest and broadest navigable river in Mindanao, with cruises passing through the riverside villages.
